subject: ela
description: Students interpret information presented in diverse media and formats and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study. Because a sixth grade worksheet or quiz cannot play audio or video, every item embeds the media as text the student can read: a described or transcribed audio clip or interview, a labeled visual such as a chart, table, timeline, diagram, map, or infographic rendered in words, a photo or video described in a caption, or a quotation from a podcast or news report. Students read the embedded media along with a short written context, then identify what the media shows, restate it in their own words, and explain how that piece of information supports, clarifies, extends, or complicates the topic, written text, or issue under study. They distinguish what the media actually presents from what they merely assume, choose the format best suited to a purpose, and judge whether a media source adds new information or simply repeats what the written text already said. Every item embeds the full media stimulus and any context it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Read and accurately interpret information presented in a non-prose format described in text, such as a chart, table, graph, timeline, diagram, map, or infographic
Interpret information from a described or transcribed audio or video source, such as an interview, news clip, podcast, or speech
Restate in your own words the central piece of information a media source presents
Explain how a media source contributes to a topic, written text, or issue under study by clarifying, supporting, extending, or complicating it
Compare information given in two different formats and explain what each adds, or which presents the information more clearly
Distinguish what a media source actually presents from an unsupported assumption or outside knowledge
Judge whether a media source provides new information or restates what a written text already said

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret a visual format
problemArchetypes.example: Media (a bar chart described in text): 'A bar chart titled Hours of Daylight by Month shows June at about 15 hours, the tallest bar, and December at about 9 hours, the shortest bar. The bars rise from January to June, then fall toward December.' Question: According to the chart, which month has the most daylight, and how does the chart show this? Answer: June, because its bar is the tallest, showing about 15 hours, more than any other month.

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret an audio or video source
problemArchetypes.example: Media (a transcript): 'In a radio interview, a marine biologist says, "We tagged forty sea turtles this season. Almost all of them returned to the very beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs."' Question: What does the interview tell you about sea turtle nesting? Answer: Sea turtles tend to return to their birth beach to lay eggs, because the biologist says almost all of the tagged turtles came back to where they hatched.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how media contributes to a topic or text
problemArchetypes.example: Context: A class is studying how cities try to reduce traffic. Written text: 'The city added new bus lanes downtown last year.' Media (an infographic described in text): 'An infographic shows that downtown bus ridership rose from 12,000 daily riders before the lanes to 19,000 after.' Question: How does the infographic contribute to the topic of reducing traffic? Answer: It adds evidence that the bus lanes worked, because the ridership numbers show more people chose the bus after the lanes were added, supporting the idea that the change reduced car traffic.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare two formats
problemArchetypes.example: Media A (a written sentence): 'The school recycled more paper each year from 2018 to 2022.' Media B (a line graph described in text): 'A line graph rises steadily from 500 pounds in 2018 to 1,400 pounds in 2022.' Question: What does the line graph show that the sentence alone does not? Answer: The graph gives the exact amounts and the steady, even rise, showing how much the recycling grew, while the sentence only says it increased.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge new information versus repetition
problemArchetypes.example: Written text: 'The volcano erupted in 1980 and covered nearby forests in ash.' Media (a photo caption): 'A photograph caption reads: Gray ash blankets fallen trees across a hillside after the 1980 eruption.' Question: Does the photo caption add new information or repeat the text? Answer: It mostly repeats the text, because it shows the same ash and fallen trees the sentence already described and adds little that is new.

Easy.description: A short, clearly described media stimulus embedded in the item, such as a simple chart, table, or short transcribed quote of roughly 2 to 4 sentences or rows (about 25 to 55 words including any context). The task is identify-level: read the media and state directly what it shows or report a single value, label, or fact it presents. Minimal inference; the correct answer is read almost straight off the described media, and distractors are clearly wrong readings.
constraints: Media is one simple format described in 2 to 4 sentences or a small table, included in the prompt
Targets a single explicit value, label, trend direction, or stated fact from the media
Identify-level task: report what the media directly shows
Distractors misread the media in obvious ways, such as naming the smallest value instead of the largest

Medium.description: A media stimulus of moderate length plus a brief written context, embedded in the item, of roughly 5 to 8 sentences or rows (about 60 to 110 words), such as a multi-bar chart, a short interview transcript, or an infographic with two or three data points. The task is analyze-level: restate the central information in the student's own words and explain how it contributes to the stated topic or text, or connect one data point to a one-step conclusion. The student must link the media to the written context, and distractors are plausible readings that are partial, off topic, or overstate what the media shows.
constraints: Media plus a short written context totals 5 to 8 sentences, rows, or data points in the prompt
Targets a one-step interpretation: how the media supports, clarifies, or relates to the topic or text
Analyze-level task: explain the contribution of the media to the topic or written text
Distractors are believable but partial, overstated, or only loosely related to the question

Hard.description: A richer media stimulus, often paired with a second format or a longer written text, embedded in the item, of roughly 9 to 14 sentences, rows, or described elements (about 120 to 200 words), such as a detailed infographic, a transcript compared with a chart, or a timeline set against an article excerpt. The task is evaluate-level: compare what two formats each contribute, judge whether the media adds new information or repeats the text, or synthesize information across the media to explain how it complicates or extends the issue under study. Requires combining more than one element and reasoning about the relationship between the media and the topic.
constraints: Media is detailed or paired with a second format or longer text, 9 to 14 sentences, rows, or elements in the prompt
Targets multi-step interpretation: compare formats, judge new versus repeated information, or synthesize across the media
Evaluate-level task: justify which format contributes more, or how the media extends or complicates the topic
Distractors include a true-but-irrelevant reading, an overstated claim the media does not support, and a detail that repeats rather than adds

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misreads the media itself, confusing the largest value with the smallest, the start of a trend with its end, or one label with another
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports December as having the most daylight because the student grabs the wrong bar, or names the lowest data point when asked for the highest

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds outside knowledge or an assumption the media does not actually present, treating what they already believe as what the source shows
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the chart proves a cause the data never states, or adds a fact about the topic the media and text never mention

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student overstates what the media shows, drawing a conclusion far larger than the single fact or data point supports
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Turns a small two-year increase into a claim that the trend will continue forever or that it is the most important factor, beyond what the media presents

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student describes what the media shows but fails to connect it to the topic, text, or issue under study, answering the wrong question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Restates the chart value correctly but never explains how it contributes to the topic, or picks an option that summarizes the media without linking it to the issue

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses repeated information with new information, treating media that echoes the text as if it adds something, or the reverse
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says a photo caption adds new evidence when it only restates the sentence above it, or calls genuinely new data a mere repeat of the text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges the wrong format as more informative, ignoring what each format actually contributes to understanding
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says a plain sentence shows the exact yearly amounts when only the graph gives the numbers, or claims the graph adds nothing when it supplies precise values the sentence lacks
